title: The Hidden Nodule: Knowing When to Stop
subtitle: Risk stratification and de-escalation in an incidental thyroid nodule
description: Which test decides whether biopsy is needed at all, ranking sonographic patterns, size thresholds that follow from pattern, FNA technique, indeterminate cytology, what a molecular test can and cannot tell you, the 2025 ATA surgical extent, and why common occult disease still does not justify prophylactic dissection.

steps.title: Step 1/10: The Report She Brings You
steps.scenario: A 45-year-old woman is found to have a 1.8 cm right thyroid nodule incidentally on neck ultrasound during an employee health check. She has no dysphagia, hoarseness, neck pain, or compressive symptoms. She has no history of neck irradiation and no family history of thyroid cancer. She brings the report to your clinic.
steps.media: Load image: Outpatient thyroid examination, physician palpating the anterior neck. Caption: none.
steps.question: Alongside a dedicated thyroid ultrasound, which single result determines whether this nodule needs a biopsy at all?

options.text: (A) Serum thyroid-stimulating hormone
(B) Serum calcitonin
(C) Serum thyroglobulin
(D) Anti-thyroid peroxidase antibody

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: A

TSH is the branch point. A suppressed TSH raises the possibility of an autonomously functioning nodule, which is very rarely malignant, and sends you to scintigraphy rather than to a needle. A normal or high TSH keeps you on the sonographic pathway.

On the distractors, all three of which are ordered in real clinics:

Calcitonin is the strongest of them. Several European groups do screen routinely to catch medullary carcinoma early, and the ATA has not recommended routine screening, citing cost-effectiveness and the problem of false positives. It is a legitimate debate, not a wrong answer by ignorance.

Thyroglobulin has no role in evaluating a nodule. Its place is post-thyroidectomy surveillance. Ordering it here is the single most common reflex error on this pathway.

Anti-TPO tells you about autoimmune thyroiditis, which changes neither the malignancy risk of this nodule nor the decision to biopsy it.

Her result: TSH 1.4 microIU/mL, normal.

steps.title: Step 2/10: The Result You Did Not Get
steps.scenario: Her TSH is normal, so you continue. Before you do, consider the path you did not take.
steps.question: Had her TSH returned suppressed at 0.05 microIU/mL, what would change?

options.text: (A) Radioiodine scintigraphy first; a hyperfunctioning nodule rarely requires FNA
(B) Proceed to FNA regardless, since a suppressed TSH raises the malignancy risk
(C) Start an antithyroid drug and repeat the ultrasound in six months before any biopsy
(D) Obtain a contrast-enhanced neck CT to assess substernal extension before biopsy

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: A

Option B inverts a relationship worth remembering: malignancy risk rises with higher TSH, not lower. A suppressed TSH points toward autonomy, and an autonomous nodule is very seldom cancer. Residents get this backwards because suppressed sounds abnormal and abnormal sounds dangerous.

Option C treats the biochemistry and abandons the nodule. Option D carries a specific harm that otolaryngologists should own: an iodinated contrast load saturates the thyroid and can delay scintigraphy or radioiodine therapy for weeks to months. Ordering contrast before you know the functional status is a mistake you cannot undo by cancelling the scan.

Back to this patient: TSH normal, so scintigraphy is not indicated and the pathway is sonographic.

steps.title: Step 3/10: Ranking the Patterns
steps.scenario: You perform the ultrasound yourself rather than reading the report. Sonographic risk stratification is a pattern-based judgment, not a checklist of individual features.
steps.media: Load image: Longitudinal and transverse grayscale images of a right thyroid nodule, unannotated. Caption: 'Right lobe, 12 MHz linear probe.'
steps.question: Which of these four sonographic descriptions carries the highest malignancy risk?

options.text: (A) Solid, hypoechoic, irregular margins, punctate echogenic foci, taller than wide
(B) Solid, isoechoic, smooth margins, with a thin peripheral hypoechoic halo
(C) Mixed cystic and solid, with an eccentric solid component and smooth margins
(D) Spongiform, with microcystic spaces occupying more than half the volume

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: A

Every option here is a real pattern with a real risk figure, which is the point. Marked hypoechogenicity, irregular or lobulated margins, microcalcifications, and a taller-than-wide shape together define the high-suspicion pattern, with a malignancy risk above 70 to 90 percent.

B is intermediate suspicion, roughly 10 to 20 percent. C is low suspicion, roughly 5 to 10 percent. D is very low suspicion, under 3 percent. None of them is zero, and none of them is absurd.

Design note for the reader: the earlier version of this question offered a purely cystic nodule as a distractor. Nobody chooses it, so the item measured nothing. An item that can be answered without knowing thyroid ultrasound is not an item.

Her nodule matches pattern A, measures 1.8 cm, and there are no sonographically abnormal cervical nodes.

Guideline note: sonographic risk stratification comes from the 2015 ATA nodule guidelines and ACR TI-RADS. It does not come from the 2025 ATA guidelines, which cover differentiated thyroid cancer only and deliberately exclude nodules.

steps.title: Step 4/10: The Threshold Follows the Pattern
steps.scenario: You have a high-suspicion nodule measuring 1.8 cm.
steps.question: At what size does FNA become indicated for a nodule with this sonographic pattern?

options.text: (A) 1 cm or larger
(B) 1.5 cm or larger
(C) 2 cm or larger
(D) Any size, since the pattern alone justifies sampling

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: A

The threshold is not a single number, it moves with the pattern. High and intermediate suspicion, 1 cm. Low suspicion, 1.5 cm. Very low suspicion, 2 cm, with observation a reasonable alternative. Purely cystic nodules do not require FNA at all.

Option D is the first appearance of the habit this case is really about. It sounds cautious. It is the reasoning that leads to biopsying subcentimeter nodules, finding microcarcinomas that were never going to matter, and committing a healthy 45-year-old to an operation and a lifetime of surveillance. Thresholds exist because more sampling is not the same as better care.

Her 1.8 cm high-suspicion nodule clears the threshold. Proceed to FNA.

steps.title: Step 5/10: The Student and the Big Needle
steps.scenario: The patient consents to ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration. While you set up, a medical student hands you an 18-gauge core needle and says: "If we get cyst fluid, we should send all of it for cytology to improve the yield."
steps.media: Load video: Ultrasound-guided FNA, transverse approach, needle tip visualized within the nodule. 10 seconds, muted.
steps.question: Which statement about needle choice and cystic fluid is most correct?

options.text: (A) Use a 25 to 27 gauge needle; aspirating cyst fluid may relieve symptoms, but cytology of the fluid itself adds little
(B) Use a 25 to 27 gauge needle, and send the cyst fluid for cytology since it may carry diagnostic cells
(C) Use an 18 gauge core needle as first-line, since it lowers the nondiagnostic rate
(D) Use a 25 to 27 gauge needle, and proceed to diagnostic lobectomy if the first pass is nondiagnostic

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: A

Standard technique is a 5 to 10 mL syringe with a 25 to 27 gauge needle and roughly five seconds of needle undulation within the lesion. Fine needles bleed less, and blood dilution is a major cause of nondiagnostic samples, which is why bigger is not better here.

Option C is not absurd, and that is deliberate. Core needle biopsy does have a role in selected situations, including repeatedly nondiagnostic nodules and suspected lymphoma or anaplastic disease where architecture matters. It is not a first-line tool for a routine nodule.

Option D is the same reflex as the last step wearing different clothes. A nondiagnostic FNA is managed with a repeat FNA after an interval, not with an operation. Going to surgery for a diagnosis you have not yet tried twice to obtain is how a benign nodule becomes a hemithyroidectomy.

On the cyst fluid specifically: aspirating it can shrink the nodule and relieve symptoms, but the fluid is usually acellular or full of macrophages. Sample the solid component under ultrasound guidance instead, which is where the answer lives.

steps.title: Step 6/10: Bethesda III
steps.scenario: One week later the cytology returns as atypia of undetermined significance, Bethesda category III. The patient calls, anxious, and asks what this means and what happens next.
steps.media: Load image: Cytology slide, Diff-Quik stain, follicular cells with mild nuclear atypia. Caption: 'Fine needle aspirate, right thyroid nodule.'
steps.question: What is the appropriate next step?

options.text: (A) Repeat FNA, molecular testing, or continued surveillance, chosen according to sonographic and clinical risk
(B) Diagnostic lobectomy, since indeterminate cytology cannot be resolved by further sampling
(C) Total thyroidectomy, since the malignancy risk of Bethesda III exceeds 50 percent
(D) Reassurance and a repeat ultrasound in twelve months

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: A

Bethesda III carries a risk of malignancy of roughly 13 to 30 percent. That number is the whole answer. It is high enough that D, discharging her for a year with a high-suspicion nodule, is unsafe. It is low enough that B and C commit most of these patients to an unnecessary operation.

Option B was standard practice for years and remains the default in many units, which is exactly why it is here. Option C is a base-rate error: it treats an indeterminate result as though it were a positive one. Seven or eight of every ten patients in her position do not have cancer.

Given a high-suspicion sonographic pattern, molecular testing is the reasonable next move for her.

Guideline note: the Bethesda System risk figures come from the third edition, 2023, not from any ATA guideline.

steps.title: Step 7/10: What a Molecular Test Actually Buys You
steps.scenario: You send the aspirate for molecular testing. Before the result comes back, be clear with yourself about what each possible answer would mean.
steps.media: Load image: Molecular test report, result panel redacted. Caption: 'Report header only.'
steps.question: Which statement best describes what a benign molecular result would do for this patient?

options.text: (A) It has a high negative predictive value, allowing surveillance rather than diagnostic surgery in most patients
(B) It confirms the nodule is benign, and no further ultrasound follow-up is needed
(C) It reliably predicts the extent of surgery required if malignancy is later found
(D) Its predictive performance is the same regardless of the sonographic risk pattern

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: A

The commercially available panels are built as rule-out tests. Their negative predictive value in indeterminate cytology is high, which is what allows a patient to be observed instead of operated on. Their positive predictive value is considerably lower, so a positive result is a reason to plan surgery, not a diagnosis.

Option D is the most instructive wrong answer and the one senior learners get wrong. Predictive values depend on pre-test probability. A benign molecular result in a very-low-suspicion nodule is strongly reassuring; the same result in a nodule with the high-suspicion pattern this patient has is less so, because the disease prevalence in that group is higher. The test does not know what the ultrasound looked like. You do, and you have to combine them.

Option B overreads a negative test into a discharge. Option C confuses a diagnostic tool with a staging one.

This is the same reasoning error the last step tested, and it will appear once more before the case ends.

steps.title: Step 8/10: Reading the Panel
steps.scenario: The molecular report returns positive. You now need to interpret which alteration was found and what weight to give it.
steps.question: Which single alteration, if detected, is most specific for papillary thyroid carcinoma?

options.text: (A) BRAF V600E
(B) An RAS point mutation
(C) A TERT promoter mutation
(D) PAX8/PPARG rearrangement

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: A

BRAF V600E is close to diagnostic. Its specificity for papillary carcinoma approaches 99 percent, so a positive result effectively settles the diagnosis before surgery.

Every distractor here is a genuine thyroid alteration, which is what makes the item work:

RAS mutations are the classic trap. They are common in papillary carcinoma of follicular variant, but they also appear in benign follicular adenomas and in NIFTP. High sensitivity, poor specificity, and a positive RAS result does not confirm cancer.

TERT promoter mutations are prognostic rather than diagnostic. They mark aggressive behavior, particularly alongside BRAF, and they change your risk conversation rather than your diagnosis.

PAX8/PPARG points toward follicular neoplasms, not papillary carcinoma.

The earlier version of this question offered BRCA1/2 and BCR-ABL as distractors. No otolaryngology resident has ever selected those, so the item tested nothing but the ability to recognise a breast gene and a leukemia gene.

Her result: BRAF V600E positive. This is papillary thyroid carcinoma.

steps.title: Step 9/10: How Much Thyroid Comes Out
steps.scenario: Papillary thyroid carcinoma, 1.8 cm, clinical T1b N0 M0. No gross extrathyroidal extension on ultrasound, the contralateral lobe is sonographically normal, and there are no suspicious lymph nodes. She asks whether the whole thyroid has to come out.
steps.media: Load image: Side-by-side diagram of thyroid lobectomy and total thyroidectomy. Caption: none.
steps.question: According to the 2025 ATA guidelines, what is the recommended surgical extent?

options.text: (A) Lobectomy
(B) Total thyroidectomy, to permit radioiodine and thyroglobulin surveillance
(C) Total thyroidectomy, because BRAF V600E positivity independently warrants it
(D) Active surveillance without surgery, given the tumor is under 2 cm

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: A

The 2025 ATA guidelines state that for tumors smaller than 2 cm without gross extrathyroidal extension or metastases, lobectomy should be the first treatment of choice when surgery is indicated, provided there are no bilateral tumors or other reasons to remove the contralateral lobe. This is a strong recommendation with moderate certainty of evidence. Lobectomy may also be the recommended initial strategy for low-risk unilateral tumors of 2 to 4 cm.

This is a real shift. In 2009 total thyroidectomy was recommended for nearly all cancers above 1 cm. In 2015 lobectomy became an option. In 2025 it became the recommendation.

On the distractors: B reverses the logic by choosing an operation in order to enable an adjuvant treatment she does not need. C is a belief many surgeons hold, but BRAF positivity alone does not change the recommended extent in an otherwise low-risk tumor. D applies the right concept to the wrong size, since active surveillance is discussed for low-risk tumors of 1 cm or less, not for a 1.8 cm cT1b.

Worth knowing for your audience: the 2025 guidelines cover differentiated thyroid cancer only. Thyroid nodules were deliberately excluded from scope, so everything in Steps 1 through 7 of this case is governed by other documents. Citing 2025 ATA for nodule workup is a mistake an examiner will catch.

Reference: Ringel MD, Sosa JA, Baloch Z, et al. 2025 American Thyroid Association management guidelines for adult patients with differentiated thyroid cancer. Thyroid. 2025;35(8):841-985.

steps.title: Step 10/10: While You Are In There
steps.scenario: You have agreed on a right lobectomy. In the pre-operative visit her husband asks: "Since you are already operating, can you take out the lymph nodes in that area too, just to be safe?"
steps.media: Load image: Central compartment level VI anatomy, with recurrent laryngeal nerve and parathyroid glands labeled. Caption: 'Level VI.'
steps.question: For this clinically node-negative T1b tumor, what do you recommend?

options.text: (A) Recommend against it, since it does not improve long-term outcomes in cN0 T1 to T2 disease and adds nerve and parathyroid risk
(B) Perform an ipsilateral central dissection, since the morbidity is acceptable and it refines recurrence risk staging
(C) Perform a bilateral central dissection, since occult nodal disease is present in a large proportion of these patients
(D) Defer, and perform a completion dissection later if surveillance thyroglobulin rises

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: A

The 2025 ATA guidelines more strongly discourage prophylactic central compartment dissection for clinically node-negative T1 to T2 disease, on the grounds that it does not improve long-term outcomes while it does increase the risk of recurrent laryngeal nerve injury and hypoparathyroidism. For larger cN0 tumors it may be considered, with limited evidence. Therapeutic dissection remains indicated when nodal involvement is identified.

Now the part worth sitting with. Option C states something true. Occult central nodal metastases are found in up to half of clinically node-negative papillary carcinoma patients eligible for lobectomy. That prevalence is real, and it is the reason this operation feels justified in the moment.

It still does not follow. A finding can be common and removing it can still fail to help, because most of that occult disease never becomes clinically relevant, while every dissection carries a nerve and a parathyroid risk that is immediate and sometimes permanent. Prevalence is not benefit. This is the same reasoning error as Steps 4, 5, 6, and 7, and it is the one this case exists to teach.

Option B is the argument for staging information. It is honest, and the guidelines answer it: the information does not change outcomes enough to justify the morbidity in this group.

Option D misunderstands post-lobectomy surveillance. After lobectomy, serial thyroglobulin monitoring is not recommended, because the remaining lobe produces it. Ultrasound every one to three years is the follow-up, not a thyroglobulin trend.

Debriefing question for the group: her husband asked a reasonable question and the answer is no. How do you say that in a way he accepts?
